facts.fact_text: On 10 February 2006, Hyde Park (the first applicant) applied to the Chişinău Municipal Council for authorisation to hold a peaceful demonstration in front of the Parliament building on 25 February 2006.

The peaceful demonstration for which Hyde Park (the first applicant) sought authorisation was intended to protest against the 'non-transparent' manner of organising the Eurovision song contest in Moldova.
On 21 February 2006, the Chişinău Municipal Council rejected Hyde Park's (the first applicant's) application to hold a demonstration in front of the Parliament building on 25 February 2006.
On 24 February 2006, the Chişinău Court of Appeal dismissed the applicants' action challenging the Chişinău Municipal Council's refusal to authorise the demonstration.
The Chişinău Court of Appeal found that the Chişinău Municipal Council had lawfully rejected Hyde Park's (the first applicant's) application to hold a demonstration.
The Chişinău Court of Appeal upheld all the reasons relied upon by the Chişinău Municipal Council for rejecting Hyde Park's (the first applicant's) application.

The Chişinău Court of Appeal gave a new reason in favour of the Chişinău Municipal Council's decision not to authorise the demonstration, namely that Hyde Park (the first applicant) had failed to correctly indicate the aim of its protest in its request for authorisation.
On 28 June 2006, the Supreme Court of Justice dismissed the applicant's appeal on points of law against the Chişinău Court of Appeal's judgment of 24 February 2006.

Section 6(1) of the Assemblies Act of 21 June 1995 provides that assemblies shall not impede the normal use of public highways, road traffic and the operation of economic undertakings.

Section 6(1) of the Assemblies Act of 21 June 1995 provides that assemblies shall not degenerate into acts of violence capable of endangering the public order and the physical integrity and life of persons or their property.
Section 7 of the Assemblies Act of 21 June 1995 provides that assemblies shall be suspended in circumstances including denial and defamation of the State and of the people.

Section 7 of the Assemblies Act of 21 June 1995 provides that assemblies shall be suspended in circumstances including incitement to war or aggression and incitement to hatred on ethnic, racial or religious grounds.

Section 8(1) of the Assemblies Act of 21 June 1995 provides that assemblies may be conducted in squares, streets, parks and other public places in cities, towns and villages, and also in public buildings.

Section 8(2) of the Assemblies Act of 21 June 1995 provides that it is forbidden to conduct an assembly in the buildings of the public authorities, the local authorities, prosecutors' offices, the courts or companies with armed security.

Section 8(3)(a) of the Assemblies Act of 21 June 1995 provides that it is forbidden to conduct assemblies within fifty metres of the parliament building, the residence of the president of Moldova, the seat of the government, the Constitutional Court and the Supreme Court of Justice.

Section 8(3)(b) of the Assemblies Act of 21 June 1995 provides that it is forbidden to conduct assemblies within twenty-five metres of the buildings of the central administrative authority, the local public authorities, courts, prosecutors' offices, police stations, prisons and social rehabilitation institutions, military installations, railway stations, airports, hospitals, companies which use dangerous equipment and machines, and diplomatic institutions.
Section 8(4) of the Assemblies Act of 21 June 1995 provides that free access to the premises of the institutions listed in section 8(3) shall be guaranteed.
Section 8(5) of the Assemblies Act of 21 June 1995 provides that the local public authorities may, if the organisers agree, establish places or buildings for permanent assemblies.
Section 11(1) of the Assemblies Act of 21 June 1995 provides that not later than fifteen days prior to the date of the assembly, the organiser shall submit a notification to the Municipal Council.
Section 11(2) of the Assemblies Act of 21 June 1995 provides that the prior notification shall indicate the name of the organiser of the assembly and the aim of the assembly.
Section 11(2) of the Assemblies Act of 21 June 1995 provides that the prior notification shall indicate the date, starting time and finishing time of the assembly.
Section 11(2) of the Assemblies Act of 21 June 1995 provides that the prior notification shall indicate the location of the assembly and the access and return routes.

Section 11(2) of the Assemblies Act of 21 June 1995 provides that the prior notification shall indicate the approximate number of participants.
Section 11(2) of the Assemblies Act of 21 June 1995 provides that the prior notification shall indicate the persons who are to ensure and answer for the sound conduct of the assembly.
Section 11(2) of the Assemblies Act of 21 June 1995 provides that the prior notification shall indicate the services the organiser of the assembly asks the Municipal Council to provide.

Section 11(3) of the Assemblies Act of 21 June 1995 provides that if the situation so requires, the Municipal Council may alter certain aspects of the prior notification with the agreement of the organiser of the assembly.

Section 12(1) of the Assemblies Act of 21 June 1995 provides that the prior notification shall be examined by the local government of the town or village at the latest five days before the date of the assembly.

Section 12(2) of the Assemblies Act of 21 June 1995 provides that when the prior notification is considered at an ordinary or extraordinary meeting of the Municipal Council, the discussion shall deal with the form, timetable, location and other conditions for the conduct of the assembly, and the decision taken shall take account of the specific situation.

Section 12(6) of the Assemblies Act of 21 June 1995 provides that the local authorities can reject an application to hold an assembly only if, after having consulted the police, they have obtained convincing evidence that the provisions of sections 6 and 7 of the Assemblies Act will be breached with serious consequences for society.

Section 15(1) of the Assemblies Act of 21 June 1995 provides that the organiser of the assembly can challenge the refusal in the administrative courts.
